instructions:
INTENT — The email must read like it was written by a person who spent thirty seconds on the prospect's site, not like a template. One idea, one tone, no stock phrases. The prospect is the subject of the sentences: more "you" than "I".

SHAPE — Every email follows exactly this form, four one-sentence paragraphs, one blank line between each, nothing else:

Hi Marc,

Saw that Foxglove runs cold email for e-commerce brands.

If you pay per seat for data you barely use, that adds up.

Your list comes back with verified emails and phones, and you pay only for filled rows.

Want me to run 100 of your rows first, free?

Eliasse

Never write a number, a section heading, a bullet, or an extra blank line. The body runs 45 to 65 words. No sentence over 16 words, no word a fourteen-year-old would not know.

SUBJECT — 2 to 4 words, all lowercase, no punctuation. It contains the prospect's company name or their trade, never ours, never "partnership", "collab", "x", "offer", "quick question", and never a first name alone. Examples: "foxglove lead lists", "your list building", "question on foxglove".

FIRST SENTENCE — An observation starting with "Saw that", "On your site," or "You run". It says what the company does, with one precise detail read from the site: a named client type, a specific service, a city. The word "businesses" is banned, as are "bespoke", "tailored", any date, any headcount, any figure, any hiring, and any client the site does not name. If the site gives no precise detail, write only the trade and the city: "Saw that you run cold email out of Austin." Never a compliment.

SECOND SENTENCE — The problem, in conditional form, never an assertion about how the prospect works. One or the other: "If you pay per seat for data you barely use, that adds up." or "If half the emails on a list bounce, the campaign pays for it."

THIRD SENTENCE — The result for them first, then what actually happens, and it ends with "you pay only for filled rows".

FOURTH SENTENCE — A closed question that asks for a reply, not a slot: "Want me to run 100 of your rows first, free?" or "Worth trying on your next list?". No other wording. NEVER write "Open to a chat?" or "Open to discussing?". No slot and no link in the first email.

OFFER — I sell contact data per record, not seats and not a subscription. Send a list of names, domains or LinkedIn URLs, it comes back with verified work emails and direct dials, and only filled rows are charged. Never name a price, a plan or a credit. Never write "AI", never name a competitor, never mention an API, an integration or a dashboard. Never ask them to sign up.
followup_instructions:
LENGTH — The first follow-up may run to four sentences, because it carries the free sample. Every later one is two sentences maximum. Same shape as the first email: one sentence per paragraph, a blank line between each, no sentence over 16 words.

BANS — Same as the first email, plus the openers. NEVER write "following up", "just following up", "bumping this", "circling back" or "quick nudge". Never write "AI", never name a competitor, never name a paid price, a plan or a subscription.

THE FREE GRANT — The signup credits are the one number allowed, and the only offer a follow-up may add: 1,000 credits on signup, no card. State only what those credits actually buy. A work email costs 10 credits and a mobile number costs 50, so 1,000 credits is 100 work emails, or 20 mobile numbers, or a mix. Never promise a count the grant does not cover, and never imply the two can both be had in full.

THE ASK — Ask them to run part of their own list and count the matches themselves. The hit rate is the objection, so let them measure it rather than claiming a figure. Never quote a match rate, a coverage percentage or a database size.

LINK — A link is allowed from the first follow-up onwards, never in the first email. It points at the product domain, never at the sending domain.

SEQUENCE — Add one new fact per touch and never repeat the offer. The last email asks for a yes or a no, and means it.
